#4463. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

Your next Mercedes-Benz could solve an annoying issue with snow-covered cars.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Two Porsche 911s at SEMA Ditch Their Flat-Sixes for Ferrari and Chevy V8s

Winter is around the corner, which means contending with issues like increasing battery failures, troublesome engine starts, and fitting snow chains in more extreme conditions. There’s another annoyance that comes with winter driving, particularly for those who live in areas that experience heavy snowfall. Opening a car door can often lead to snow falling on your seat, creating a mess and potentially damaging your upholstery. Automakers are constantly working on solutions to everyday inconveniences like this one, and Mercedes-Benz has just filed a patent for a seemingly simple nozzle system that can quickly remove snow from the roof or doors, before it has a chance to fall inside the car.

The German patent was discovered by Car Moses and published on October 29, 2026. It describes a roof element with nozzles, presumably built into the area close to where a roof rail would be positioned. Air is blown through these nozzles to remove snow sitting on the vehicle, particularly in areas above or around the door opening, where snow can accumulate and fall into the interior.

A compressed air supply delivers the blast of air needed to remove the snow, but the document does not detail the pressure, flow rate, compressor type, or whether the air is heated. Heated air could partially melt the snow, but that alone wouldn’t fully alleviate the issue. A more logical expectation is that the force of the air will be sufficient to physically propel the snow off the door/roof. A simple button could be pressed to allow the snow-removal system to do its job.

By preventing snow and liquid from entering the cabin, the invention would also have the secondary benefit of protecting electronic components and control units, which could lead to expensive repairs if damaged.

The invention would be of particular value in states where it’s legally required to clear snow from the roof, hood, trunk, windows, and windshield before driving, as in New Jersey. The Mercedes solution won’t clear snow from all these areas, but it should make at least part of the task easier.

Since any vehicle with this technology would need a compressed air supply, one likely candidate for the feature is the Mercedes-Benz E-Class All-Terrain. This luxury wagon comes with a standard air suspension, as do several other high-end Mercs. Additionally, the patent also includes a sketch of what is obviously a Mercedes wagon.

However, there’s no reason that Mercedes couldn’t install a dedicated air supply for the snow-removal nozzles, whether or not the vehicle in question has an air suspension. If the feature ever makes it to production, Mercedes may choose to bundle the option into a Winter Package. Currently, the E-Class All-Terrain can be equipped with a Winter Package for $450, which includes a heated steering wheel and heated windshield washers. The snow-removing nozzles would be a sensible addition, assuming the system can be fitted at a price that makes sense for the automaker and buyers.

Maintaining your car's heating and cooling system for winter

Just like you wouldn’t wait until the hottest day of the year to test your air conditioning system, you shouldn’t wait until the temperatures drop to ensure your heating system is prepared for the season ahead.

A patent application is no guarantee that a particular feature will make it to production. Automakers are constantly innovating behind the scenes and like to secure the rights to certain technologies, whether or not they end up being used. It’s obvious that people living in snowy states like Vermont, Alaska, and New York could benefit from the tech. Mercedes is also in a position to charge a premium for the feature, as German automakers are known to do. We’ll now have to wait and see if the innovation makes it into your next GLE SUV or S-Class sedan.

#4461. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

Tesla’s Megapacks are bringing big batteries to the grid, but you can get the same benefits at home by pairing solar with storage. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4460. 1985 Ford F-250 Restomod Sends Raptor Brand to the ’80s at SEMA

Matt Johnson’s 1985 F-250 Raptor-inspired build was backed by Ford Performance and will be part of Ford’s display at SEMA this year.

Ford’s first Raptor didn’t arrive until 2008 at the 41st Baja 1000 in Ensenada, Mexico. The high-performance F-150 SVT Raptor-R had a podium finish, and the Raptor name continues to grace the widened bodywork of some of Ford’s most powerful pickups.

But imagine if Raptor had come around about two decades earlier. It might’ve looked like Matt Johnson’s Raptor-inspired 1985 F-250, which is getting a huge reveal at Ford’s SEMA booth this year.

The F-250 project actually started with an old Toyota Land Cruiser, which Johnson had planned to put an EcoBoost engine into. A call to Ford Racing Parts led to discussions about a collaboration between the automaker and Johnson, who restores older off-roading vehicles and documents the process on social media.

See all results for new 2027 Ford Super Duty for sale near 22932

A few months later, Ford suggested putting a small-block Heritage motor in the Land Cruiser. Johnson bounced back with a photo of a 1985 F-250 with a blown engine that had been sitting behind his shop. He felt the small-block was better suited for a classic Ford, and the bullnose F-250 seemed like a perfect candidate.

Soon, Johnson’s $800 shop truck, called Norma Jeane, was getting a full makeover backed by Ford Performance. The truck’s original engine was replaced with Ford Racing’s 575-hp 460-cubic-inch Boss V-8. He paired the small-block with a Ford R680 six-speed automatic transmission.

Johnson documented the transformation through a 92-part series on social media. His daily updates covered everything, from installing a custom-made suspension kit to weatherstripping the windows. Though a lot of the truck is now brand new, the F-250 maintains its distinctly ‘80s qualities, right down to the hubcaps and vintage-style stereo.

The build was originally meant to be completed in 40 days, but when Ford proposed the idea of bringing it to SEMA, that 40-day timeline shifted to a much longer saga. Along the way, Johnson has accumulated 425,000 followers on Instagram and even more on Facebook under his Doc Johnson Restorations shop account. His latest post shows the F-250 getting loaded into a transport truck and beginning the journey from his small shop in Klamath Falls, Oregon, to SEMA in Las Vegas.

“Honestly, it’s a crazy story, and I feel blessed to be a part of it,” Johnson said in a press release. “The truck—and the project itself—took on a life of its own. In many ways, I’m just along for the ride.” Johnson and his Raptor-inspired F-250 will be a part of Ford’s display at SEMA, which takes place November 3-6 in Las Vegas, Nevada.

#4459. 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Harkens Back to a Simpler Time

Harley-Davidson’s new entry-level motorcycle resurrects a classic name and its single-cylinder formula.

Given the price of, well, everything these days, affordability and accessibility are unsurprisingly hot buzzwords in the motorcycle industry. And brands that’ve embraced them are reaping the benefits. Bikes like Triumph’s 400 range and Royal Enfield’s 350 range—lightweight, inexpensive, modest-capacity single-cylinder—are practically flying off showroom floors. Up until now, that’s described nothing in Harley-Davidson’s stable, at least for US riders. But that changes with the 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440.

See all results for used cars for sale near 47448

While the Bar and Shield basically bleeds V-twins, the brand hasn’t only made two-cylinder bikes. Its earliest models, often called “Silent Gray Fellows,” had single-cylinder engines. And if the new Sprint 440’s name seems familiar to you, it’s because Harley sold single-powered bikes with that nameplate in the 1960s and 1970s.

While those Sprints were built in Italy, the US-market Sprint 440s will be built in Harley’s York, Pennsylvania factory. Admittedly, this new Sprint technically derives from the single-cylinder Harley that’s already been on sale elsewhere for several years: the X440 developed together with the Indian company Hero MotoCorp. But still, don’t cry heresy, Milwaukee faithful.

It might use a vintage name and manufacturing formula, but the 2027 Sprint 440 is a thoroughly modern Harley-Davidson. Its 440cc two-valve air/oil-cooled single-cylinder engine—fuel-injected, unlike the carbureted original Sprints—makes 27 hp and 28 pound-feet, sent to the rear wheel via a slip-assist clutch and six-speed transmission. That rear wheel is 17 inches in diameter, with the front being 19 inches; both are cast aluminum. And when the Sprint needs to stop, er, sprinting, you’ve got ABS-equipped disc brakes.

If that doesn’t seem like enough scream for this eagle, know that the Royal Enfield Meteor 350 cruiser’s 394cc single-cylinder engine makes 20 hp and 20 pound-feet. Also, according to the spec sheets, the Sprint 440 is slightly lighter: a claimed 412 pounds to the Meteor 350’s 421 pounds. The Sprint is that much lighter than the upcoming Triumph Bonneville T40 as well, though the Triumph’s 398cc liquid-cooled single makes 30 hp (and other Triumph 400 models make around 40 hp). But, in another accessibility nod, the Meteor 350’s and Bonneville T4’s seats are 30.1 and 32.2 inches high, respectively, while Harley claims a 26.4-inch laden seat height for the Sprint. All three of these bikes have preload-adjustable dual rear shocks, though unlike the other two, the Sprint 440’s forks are inverted.

See all results for used cars for sale near 47448

Moving on, the 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 has a color TFT display (something quickly becoming de rigeur). The 3.5-inch circular gauge shows a speedometer, tachometer, odometer, and trip meter as well as the usual warning lights and turn signals. Those turn signals, like the headlight and taillight, are LED. And there’s one of the other modern motorcycling necessities, a USB-C charging port, above the headlight. Additionally, Harley-Davidson will offer numerous accessories for the Sprint 440, including a windshield, engine guard, saddlebags, and (predictably) skull adornments. Also, if the regular seat isn’t the right height, there will be multiple seat options to dial in your proper fit.

OK, accessibility seems fine, but what about that affordability? When Harley-Davidson first announced it was resurrecting the Sprint, it claimed the bike would cost around $6000. As of this writing, U.S. pricing hasn’t been revealed. However, in Canada, the Sprint 440 will cost $8499 CAD, which is about $6100 at current exchange rates. That’s roughly $1000 more than a 2027 Royal Enfield Meteor 350, though it’s around what Triumph charges for its 400 models.

But, crucially, it’s almost $4000 less expensive than Harley’s current entry-level model, the 975cc Nightster. And while everything’s expensive these days, four grand still buys quite a bit of gasoline for riding. We’ll just have to wait until spring 2027 to see if the Sprint 440 hits the ground running.

After discovering car magazines and Fast and Furious movies in high school, Matthew Skwarczek wanted to create cleaner fuels to keep automobiles around. That's how he found himself first at MotorBiscuit and then at C/D. Today, when he’s not reading, he’s daydreaming on Bring a Trailer, backpacking, or riding his motorcycle or bicycle.

Ford Crams The Most Powerful OEM Crate Engine Ever Made Into New Bronco Concept

Ford puts a 7.3-liter supercharged V8 monster into a Bronco like no other.

Winter Weather Advisory Issued for Up to 11 Inches of Snow Across Colorado Through Thursday

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

As if the Ford Megazilla crate engine wasn’t already crazy enough at 7.3 liters of displacement, the Megazilla 2.0 engine added a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger to the equation, unlocking over 1,000 horsepower. But now Ford Racing Parts has taken the recipe even further, showing off a new take on Megazilla 2.0 at the 2026 SEMA Show. Crammed under the hood of a Bronco dubbed Frostwarden is “the most powerful crate engine ever created by an automaker,” boasts Ford, producing over 1,200 hp and over 1,000 lb-ft of torque, and it’s taken a lot of extra engineering to ensure the engine can deliver those numbers reliably.

Ford is quick to point out that creating Megazilla 2.0 wasn’t as simple as bolting a supercharger to Megazilla 1.0, noting that the program required developing a stronger block, a camshaft specifically designed to work with a supercharger, beefier pistons, bigger fuel injectors, a different belt drive and damper, and the Gen 6 version of Whipple’s 3.0-liter blower, with a bright blue painted cover. But an engine sitting on a stand in a SEMA hall struggles to stand out, impressive as it may be, and that’s why the Frostwarden Bronco was built. The idea was based around a Bronco used for search and rescue operations in Arctic conditions, and that means the off-roader needed more than just a glow-up under the hood.

In association with Kincer Chassis in Tennessee, the widened Bronco was given portal gear lifts from 74Weld, custom 18-inch Weld bead-lock wheels wrapped in 42-inch BFGoodrich rubber, steel bumpers (with a winch in front), and custom Bilstein dampers. Driveline hardware was upgraded with help from Dana, and various accessories were added to the roof and tailgate, including traction board holders from RTR and extra lighting from Rigid. With a black-and-mustard theme on the exterior, the cabin was given similar treatment, along with additional carbon fiber highlights. Altogether, it looks as good as an OEM vehicle that might be offered on a dealer floor, and we quite like the dual-exit exhaust tips, but the Frostwarden, like other SEMA concepts, is not destined for series production.

The Frostwarden is basically one big, expensive advertisement for Ford Racing Parts and the scope of customization open to the Blue Oval’s products, but the main focus is undoubtedly this wild new version of the Megazilla supercharged V8. While a production vehicle with such an engine may not be feasible, builds like this help enthusiasts envision what is possible in a Ford, encouraging drag racers, drifters, off-roaders, and more to explore buying a one-size-fits-all engine regardless of their specific motoring application. So what does it cost? Ford has not said, but a naturally aspirated Megazilla 1.0 starts well over $20,000, and a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger costs anything from $7,000 to $15,000, so Megazilla 2.0 will surely be in the $30k bracket.

#4457. Kia racks up another record month as its new $30K electric SUV hits dealers

Kia is eyeing its fourth consecutive annual US sales record after another record-breaking October. With the new 2027 EV3 arriving, Kia is “confident” the momentum will carry into Q4 and well into 2027.

“With six consecutive months of record-breaking sales, Kia is accelerating toward a fourth straight annual sales record,” Kia America vice president of sales Eric Watson said on Tuesday.

Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best October sales month ever.

Kia said electrified and hybrid vehicles drove the growth, with sales up 112% and 114% YOY, both setting new sales records.

Several Kia models posted strong YOY sales growth, including the three-row electric EV9 (+111%), Telluride (+63%), EV6 (+58%), Seltos (+43%), Sorento (+31%), Carnival (+17%), K4 (+14%), and Sportage (+12%).

Regarding its fully electric vehicles. Sales of the EV9, Kia’s three-row electric SUV, are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

Although EV6 sales rebounded slightly last month, they are still down 39% YTD, with 7,067 units sold through October.

Kia’s new entry-level electric SUV, the EV3 (check out our review), is now in showrooms nationwide. After it went on sale in mid-August, Kia sold 1,496 EV3s in its first two months.

The 2027 EV3 is Kia’s most affordable fully electric vehicle, starting at $29,890. That’s for the base EV3 Light model, which uses a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range.

Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Front-wheel-drive (FWD) models have a single 201-horsepower electric motor. Upgrading to all-wheel-drive (AWD) costs $3,200 and adds a rear electric motor for a combined 261 horsepower.

All variants have a native NACS port so that drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. Charging the 58.3 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes around 29 minutes, while the larger 81.4 kWh battery takes about 31 minutes.

Inside, all EV3 models feature Kia’s latest ccNC (connected car Navigation Cockpit) with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The setup provides nearly 30″ of combined digital screens, including a dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and touchscreen infotainment, plus a 5″ climate control display.

Kia describes the EV3 as an “entry-level EV SUV that offers many of the advanced amenities of the EV9,” but in a smaller, more affordable package.

The 2027 Kia EV9 starts at $54,990. That’s also for the base EV9 Light short-range trim, which uses a 76.1 kWh battery with up to 230 miles of range.

Higher-priced trims, including the Light Long Range, Wind, Land, and GT-Line, use a larger 99.8 kWh battery that delivers up to 305 miles of range in RWD variants.

#4456. This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.

First teased last week, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.

And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.

The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.

But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.

The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.

That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.

The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.

Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.

Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.

There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.

The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.

The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.

For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.

Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.

The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.

Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.

Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.

But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.

Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.

Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.

It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.

Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.

Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.

The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.

By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.

A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.

In the US, this could go pretty much anywhere that didn't require highway driving. Perfect one-and-a-halfth car.

The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.

Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.

Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.

For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

#4453. 6 JRPGs to Play If You Loved Final Fantasy Resonance

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

Final Fantasy Resonance is here, and it is already earning high praise from critics and players alike. Boasting an overwhelmingly positive score on Steam, the JRPG has been showered with acclaim for its combat systems, its compelling cast, and its triumphant return to Final Fantasy roots, serving as a love letter to fans of the franchise's 90s golden era.

If you cherished everything Rain and Lasswell's title brought to the table and want more, I have put together a list of other JRPGs to dive into if you enjoyed Final Fantasy Resonance. We have titles featuring modular Job systems, gorgeous pixel art, and secret-packed worlds that will extend your playtime far beyond the main story. It has never been a better time to be a JRPG fan.

Final Fantasy Resonance traces its lineage back to Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, and like many mobile gacha projects, it wears its mainline references and influences proudly. You know who else excels at wearing their JRPG influences on their sleeve? Indie developers. And speaking of phenomenal indie JRPGs, Chained Echoes is a masterclass. If you haven't played it yet, fix that immediately.

First off, Chained Echoes doesn't feature a traditional class system, so if that is your primary draw, the other entries on this list might suit you better. However, if you are looking for stunning pixel art, a gripping narrative, lovable characters, and a nostalgic trip down memory lane, whether through familiar tropes of yesteryear or simply the authentic feel of a 16-bit classic, you owe it to yourself to try Chained Echoes. Its turn-based combat loop is iconic, progression feels clean yet engaging, and its world exploration stands among the finest in the genre. It is thoroughly worth your time.

Plenty of hidden gems in the mobile world deserve a second chance.

Live A Live is delightfully unorthodox, and neither its combat layout nor its narrative structure shares much common ground with Final Fantasy Resonance. Their primary shared trait is the HD-2D visual engine. You might ask why I am recommending it here, and the answer comes down to character focus. Final Fantasy Resonance shines through its incredible cast, successfully translating gacha origins into a complete offline adventure by turning side characters into quest givers and granting them a well-deserved spotlight.

This often-overlooked SNES classic is entirely character-driven. At the start of the journey, you select from several distinct scenarios, each featuring its own protagonist, narrative arc, and setting. The structure feels episodic, but everything weaves together brilliantly by the end. Final Fantasy Resonance places that same heavy emphasis on its cast, so if character development was your favorite aspect, Live A Live will deliver in spades.

Fantasian might be one of the most underrated JRPGs on the market. Developed by Mistwalker under the direction of Hironobu Sakaguchi, the creator of Final Fantasy, Fantasian deserves far more mainstream recognition. Granted, the game originally debuted on a limited platform with Apple Arcade (where I first played it), but the release of Fantasian Neo Dimension brought it to consoles and PC, and you should definitely give it a shot.

Comparatively, the main parallel it shares with Final Fantasy Resonance is its turn-based foundation, though even the combat has its own distinct flavor. Fantasian introduces a unique trajectory targeting system where abilities feature varied area-of-effect paths. Each character follows their own skill tree, and while offering roughly three distinct build directions per party member, it lacks the deep modular customization of Resonance. Still, that comforting sense of playing a classic JRPG from a bygone era, bringing warmth to your heart as you revisit retro design sensibilities, is undisputed. If you want pure nostalgia, Fantasian is the way to go.

Our reviewer earned a platinum trophy and gave Final Fantasy Resonance a 10/10. Check out DualShockers' review of Final Fantasy Resonance.

One of my favorite parts of watching new players jump into Final Fantasy Resonance was seeing them unlock fresh Visions and map out synergy builds for their party. I could practically see the gears turning as they calculated which abilities would mesh best with each character. If that customization loop was your favorite part of the experience, I highly recommend picking up Bravely Default.

Any entry in the series will do, but both Bravely Default II and Bravely Default Flying Fairy HD Remaster will scratch that build-crafting itch (I personally find the second half of the original game a bit tedious, hence my primary recommendation for Bravely Default II). The Job system functions almost identically to Visions in Final Fantasy Resonance: the more you level up your Jobs, the wider your build options and combat potential become. Who knows, you might just discover your next favorite Bartz-style combo in Bravely Default.

If Final Fantasy Resonance left you feeling nostalgic, it is only fitting to revisit the pinnacle of pixel remaster releases. This is doubly true if you have yet to play Final Fantasy VI, as you will recognize countless references while discovering why so many fans rank the sixth entry as the franchise's absolute peak. Final Fantasy VI is simultaneously accessible and deeply complex across all of its design layers.

The combat uses the classic Active Time Battle system, but each party member has unique innate strengths that can be further customized through Espers. The story avoids focusing on a single protagonist, instead distributing screen time across an ensemble cast to build a living, captivating world. During the game's second half, the path forward is left entirely in your hands. Ultimately, you will get to experience one of the true masterpieces of the JRPG genre, or reconnect with it if you have not checked out the Pixel Remaster edition yet.

Final Fantasy Resonance proves that classic Final Fantasy ideas still work, from turn-based combat and jobs to overworld exploration and dungeons.

The most obvious choice on this list is Octopath Traveler II. While I still suggest playing the original first to avoid getting too comfortable with the sequel's refinements, nothing stops you from diving straight into the second title. Octopath Traveler II takes the foundation established by Square Enix's inaugural HD-2D release and elevates every aspect, from storytelling and combat mechanics to visual polish.

Octopath Traveler II previously held the highest review score for an HD-2D title before Final Fantasy Resonance arrived, which speaks volumes about both games' quality. Both titles offer unmatched character customization, with the Visions in Final Fantasy Resonance mirroring the flexibility, dynamism, and build variety found in Octopath Traveler II's Job system. It offers more HD-2D charm, more heart, and endless fun

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Mercedes-Benz Wants To Blow Snow Off Your Car Before You Open The Door

I-70 drivers face snow through Wednesday’s evening commute, and the state’s traction law now applies to two-wheel drive cars too.

Kia's Telluride Is Closing In On The Sportage's U.S. Sales Crown

Shaq Spent $1.3 Million on 3 Rolls-Royces to Spite a Salesman

Up to 11 inches of snow is forecast over high terrain into Thursday morning under new winter weather advisories from the National Weather Service. Forecasters expect slippery roads during the Wednesday evening commute, and when the state activates the traction law on the mountain highways covered by the advisories, every passenger car has to meet its traction requirements, either with qualifying tires or with chains or an approved alternative traction device.

NWS Denver has the winter weather advisory in effect from 4 p.m. ET Wednesday to 4 a.m. ET Thursday for the mountains of Summit County, the Mosquito Range, the Indian Peaks and South Park, including the Eisenhower Tunnel, Berthoud Pass, Breckenridge, Winter Park and Fairplay. Total accumulation is forecast at 3 to 10 inches, with locally higher amounts in the Mosquito Range, and the office expects slippery spots along the US 285 corridor.

Two neighboring offices run from the same hour to 7 a.m. ET Thursday. NWS Pueblo forecasts 4 to 9 inches, locally up to 11, for the Sawatch and Mosquito ranges and Pikes Peak, mostly above 11,000 feet, and says travel could be very difficult. NWS Grand Junction expects 4 to 8 inches above 10,000 feet in the Gore and Elk Mountains, covering Vail Pass, Vail and Aspen, and warns that bridges and overpasses will likely turn slick. Vail Pass remains under an advisory until 7 a.m. ET Thursday, three hours after the one covering Summit County expires.

CDOT can activate the passenger vehicle traction law on any state highway, and on I-70 between Dotsero and Morrison it applies from Sept. 1 through May 31, according to the agency. Each activation is posted on overhead message boards and the COtrip map. A new state law signed May 5 makes clear that it applies to all passenger vehicles, two-wheel drive included, not only four-wheel and all-wheel drive models, the Post Independent reports.

To comply, tires need at least 3/16 inch of tread and an all weather rating, an M+S or M/S marking, or the mountain and snowflake symbol. Cars without qualifying tires need chains or an approved alternative traction device on at least two tires, and CDOT lists the fine at $100 plus a $33 surcharge, rising to $500 plus $157 if the vehicle ends up closing a travel lane. A separate passenger vehicle chain law, which requires chains or an approved alternative traction device on every car regardless of tire type, is a last resort that CDOT last activated in March 2019. NWS Denver points drivers to cotrip.org or the 511 phone line for current road conditions.

#4450. Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more

Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.

The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.

The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.

There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.

Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that Zero hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.

With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.

And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.

The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).

That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.

Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.

We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the smallest of electric motorcycles that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.

Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.

The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.

Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as a potential gateway to motorcycle ownership.

“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.

That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.

Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.

But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.

Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.

The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.

Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.

The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.

Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.

The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.

For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.

That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.

The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.

Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.

While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.

The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.

Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.

Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.

That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.

The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.

Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.

The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.

Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.

The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.

One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.

The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.

An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.

Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.

Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.

Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.

The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.

Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging.

Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.

The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.

That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.

Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.

European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.

The latter is particularly interesting given the growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.

Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.

The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.

Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.

There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.

For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.

The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.

I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.

That’s an audience I’ve been watching grow for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.

For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.

The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.

During the late 60’s to the early 70’s the in thing in motorcycles was the street legal dirt bike. I had a 1971 model Kawasaki 125 street legal dirtbike that I bought for $525 and it was great for getting around as a kid. When this street legal type of EV bike goes below $5000 it could be the next big thing.

And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.

Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.

But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.

And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

#4449. Jeep Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept Previews the Future by Pulling from the Past

Remember the CJ-8 Scrambler? This one is like that, but with an independent front suspension and a trophy truck–inspired rear axle.

CORRECTION 11/3/26: This story has been updated to correct details about the origins of the original CJ-8 Scrambler.

Long before the Jeep Gladiator pickup truck, the Scrambler from the 1980s was the brand’s first cargo-bed-toting model. Now, Jeep has plans to resurrect the Scrambler as a production vehicle, with a new SRT concept revealed at this year’s SEMA show providing a preview.

Unlike the original CJ-8 Scrambler, which was based on a stretched CJ-7 chassis, the new Scrambler SRT concept is built on a Wrangler foundation. For the bits under the bodywork, Jeep worked with a Dakar-winning off-road driver to develop the Scrambler SRT’s suspension, which, for the first time on a Wrangler-branded vehicle, has an independent front setup. The high-travel front suspension pairs with a trophy truck–inspired rear axle, which builds on the design Jeep first showcased on the race-winning Gladiator Striker.

See all results for new 2028 Jeep Wrangler Scrambler for sale near 50317

The new Scrambler’s front end is instantly recognizable as a Jeep, though it looks a bit different from the rest of the brand’s lineup. For starters, the grille takes on a slightly retro style and sports a bit of an overbite. Then there’s the prominent hood scoop atop the engine cover and oversized fender flares, both of which are fitting for a truck wearing SRT badges. The concept is finished in a suitably loud Punk’n orange paint that gives Toyota’s Solar Octane paint a run for its money.

The goal with the Scrambler SRT, according to Tim Kuniskis, who now fills the role of head of American Brands, SRT Performance and Direct Connection, Stellantis North America, was to find out what happens when “SRT stops treating the trail as the limit and builds the ultimate open-air desert weapon.”

To that end, Jeep decided that the Scrambler SRT concept needed a V-8 under the hood. Unfortunately, we don’t know exactly which V-8 the truck is equipped with. Given the SRT badges on the sides, though, we think it’s a safe bet that the concept is rocking either the supercharged 6.2-liter Hellcat engine or the 6.4-liter Hemi 392. Either engine would provide suitable performance, but, knowing Kuniskis, the Hellcat is the likelier choice.

The Scrambler SRT concept is the first public appearance of the Scrambler name since Jeep confirmed plans for the model to return at its investor relations day back in May. When it does arrive, there will likely be a full lineup of Scramblers, with an SRT version sitting at the top of the line. The official timeline is still up in the air, as are official style and mechanical details, but the Scrambler SRT concept gives us a great preview of future production models, which we think could arrive in 2028.

The Range Rover brand was once seen as a luxury reserved for the wealthy, until Jaguar Land Rover introduced the Evoque and Velar in the 2010s. These two provided alternatives for buyers who weren’t willing to spend flagship Range Rover money but still wanted to own a vehicle from the brand. The Evoque even sold 125,364 units globally in 2014, making it one of the brand’s biggest commercial successes.

But times are changing, and now, Range Rover boss Martin Limpert has confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will be discontinued. Their production will continue into 2027, but the British luxury marque isn’t planning direct replacements. Instead, the entry-level role will be shared by the upcoming Range Rover GT and the Range Rover Sport.

This is an interesting development, given that the Range Rover GT was initially announced as the fifth member of the Range Rover family, alongside the Evoque, Velar, Range Rover Sport, and flagship Range Rover. It suggests that there may have been a change of plans, which may not come as a surprise to some, as the automaker wants to prioritize profitability rather than chase sales volume.

The plan is to prioritize more expensive, higher-margin vehicles rather than sell more units. This approach could help Range Rover avoid competing directly with growing Chinese brands that have become increasingly popular in more affordable segments. Another strategy is to sell more bespoke creations, with the company saying it doesn’t see a price ceiling for these commissions.

But this upmarket push comes at the expense of the Evoque and Velar. In the U.S., the Evoque starts at $49,900, excluding destination charges, while the Velar starts at $61,600. The Range Rover GT is expected to start at £100,000 (about $135,000 at current exchange rates) as an EV. Its Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA) platform will also accommodate a hybrid version, reportedly priced from around £90,000 ($121,000).

In the broader JLR business, the discontinuation of the Evoque and Velar could help Range Rover move even further upmarket. JLR has also repositioned Range Rover, Defender, and Discovery as distinct brands, so the latter two will continue to cater to the more attainable side of the luxury market. Jaguar, meanwhile, is rebooting as an all-electric luxury brand, starting with the Type 01.

The Range Rover and Range Rover Sport have also gained fully electric versions, though both retain the MLA-Flex platform, which supports different powertrains, including diesels.

#4447. 10 Legendary Weapons You Should Have in Borderlands 4

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Borderlands 4 has a lot of legendary weapons. With the first entire year of content for the game being done, there are now over 160 different legendary weapons that you can choose from.

This only covers the actual weapons, like legendary assault rifles and shotguns, and not the grenades, shields, and class mods you can get. When choosing a weapon, there is a lot to consider.

At this point, there are several weapons that you should have in your bank or on your character that have stayed consistently strong. If you don’t have these weapons, you should probably start farming for them in case there are future DLC plans.

Crow-Sourced is not a legendary weapon, but I am counting it anyone because it is a Pearlescent and they are more rare than legendary items in Borderlands 4. This weapon is one of the Pearlescent weapons added with the first DLC titled Mad Ellie and the Vault of the Damned.

To obtain this assault rifle, you need to make your way over to the Captain Willis boss fight in The Maelstrom. In other words, you won’t get it until the end of the DLC, but it is well worth the wait.

This weapon has the Left of the Murder ability, which makes it fire out random projectiles as you shoot it. Charging the weapon increases the number of projectiles, making it more lethal the more it is charged.

Captain Willis will give you a run for your money in the Mad Ellie and the Vault of the Damned DLC for Borderlands 4.

The Swan Song is one of those weapons that you can use to clear a room very quickly, which means it is a guarantee that you should have it on your characters. This weapon fires fast, hits hard, and even shoots cannonballs.

That’s right, you read that correctly, it first cannonballs. Thanks to its Cannonball ability, you can shoot out cannonballs from the underbarrel of this weapon. Each kill with this weapon grants additional cannonballs, with four being the maximum.

As a weapon, the Swan Song is very powerful, but the underbarrel packs a massive punch, so it is important to continuously use it as you take down enemies. Speaking of takedowns, you get this weapon from the Takedown at Hadron Abyss.

The Darkbeast is one of my go-to weapons when I create a new character. I have a level 30 version of this weapon for new characters, and I always make sure to get one at max level as well for each character.

This SMG packs a serious punch, with it often outperforming other weapons that I use on my characters. Its Parley ability makes it so bullets pierce enemies, and have a 5% chance to cause an explosion when they hit an enemy.

Thanks to this weapon's amazing fire rate, that 5% seems to proc very often, causing major damage. You will never be let down by the Darkbeast, and you can get it from Voraxis in the Coastal Bonescape.

With how I mentioned that the Darkbeast tends to outperform other weapons, there are some that still outperform it, and the Ohm I got is one of them. This is an electric legendary SMG that fires a laser at opponents, and it will absolutely destroy shields.

It has the ability Energy Transfer, which boosts its damage by 50% whenever your shield is active. However, it consumes your shield in the process. This can be prevented if you have an overshield, so any character can get massive damage with this weapon if they just have an overshield.

The best part about this ability, besides the damage, is that it doesn’t consume ammo when you have a shield either, allowing it to fire infinitely until your shield is gone. You can get this weapon from the second Ripper Queen fight.

If you want a weapon that can delete a boss’s health bar, look no further than the Hot Slugger. A few shots from this can annihilate a health bar if you have the right build.

This legendary shotgun has the Blazing Barrel ability, which gives it a 30% damage boost for 10 seconds after you get a kill. This can stack up to three times for a massive 90% damage boost if you keep getting kills.

You can stack this damage during a boss fight by killing minions and then destroy the boss’s health bar. There are multiple builds that can take advantage of this weapon, and it is amazing.

The Convergence has been around since the start of Borderlands 4 and it still stands as one of the best legendary shotguns in the game, and it is one that you can get relatively easily. It is also a gun that can carry you through many hardships.

This weapon has the Asymptotic ability, which it doesn’t give an explanation for, but you can easily tell what it does as soon as you fire the weapon. Every time you hit an enemy, additional shots converge onto that enemy dealing additional damage.

This causes the weapon to deal some massive damage to enemies. Combined with its fast fire rate, you can easily wipe out health bars in no time. This weapon is dropped from Bramblesong in the Bittervein Augur Mine.

There are many bosses in Borderlands 4, but only Bramblesong has the Convergence as a dedicated drop.

Don’t you just wish that your guns had triple the bullets that you could embed into the bodies of your enemies? Well, the Triplicate, one of the best DLC weapons, aims to deliver, as it will indeed fill your enemies full of lead.

This weapon has the Tripled ability, which makes it so additional explosive projectiles get lobbed whenever you hit an enemy. This makes the weapon overpowered, and capable of taking down groups of enemies in record time.

If you manage to get a shotgun alternate fire mode on this weapon, it will score multiple hits, allowing multiple projectiles to spawn out of the enemy, and when used against larger enemies, it is a death sentence. You can get this weapon from The Reject Prototype in the Amara and the Vile Shadow DLC.

The Golden God is amazing as long as you don’t mind continuously buying ammo for it, as it will use a ton of ammo. However, that ammo loss is okay since you will annihilate every enemy you look at.

The ability Rage make it so that the Golden Gun does not break when you hit the heat threshold. Instead, it continuously consumes greater and greater amounts of ammo until you eventually run out.

This allows you to continuously output damage at an impressive rate, but you will just use a ton of ammo in the process. This weapon can be obtained by farming Idolator Sol, which is one of the earlier bosses in the game.

Stray is a legendary sniper rifle that was available from the get-go when Borderlands 4 launched. All you needed to do was make your way over to the Tendercage Ripper Drill Site and kill the boss called Pango Bango.

Pango Bango drops three weapons, but Stray is by far the best of them. This legendary sniper rifle has the ability stray, which makes it fire two secondary bullets that home in on nearby targets.

This makes it great for clearing out crowds, and one of the best sniper rifles in the game. It is a weapon, like the others on this list, that works very well with most builds, and can be utilized by any of the characters effortlessly.

At this point, everyone should have the Bod in either their bank or on their character, as this weapon is fantastic, and is amazing for testing out builds. The reason is that is counts as every type of weapon.

The All-Arounder ability on it makes it so that it counts as a shotgun, assault rifle, sniper rifle, pistol, and SMG. This also means that it is affected by every type of damage increase, even for specific weapon types.

Even more, the damage bonuses can stack, meaning you can get the benefit of skills that increase damage for SMGs and shotguns on this weapon. To obtain the Bod, you will want to farm Axemaul in Carcadia Burn district of Dominion.

#4446. BYD’s 3,000-hp EV crashes at about 280 mph — Watch the driver escape unharmed

BYD’s electric supercar delivers an insane nearly 3,000 hp from four electric motors. During a high-speed test, the Yangwang U9 Extreme crashed at about 280 mph, but the driver walked away unharmed.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is a “dream car,” as BYD calls it, a souped-up, track-focused version of its electric hypercar.

After it became the world’s fastest production car last year, reaching a top speed of 496.22 km/h, or about 308 mph, BYD is attempting to beat it by breaking the 500 km/h (310 mph) mark.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme features the world’s first mass-produced 1,200V ultra-high-voltage platform and BYD’s e4 platform.

The quad-motor setup is the first in the world rated at 30,000 rpm, BYD said, delivering nearly 3,000 hp (3,000 PS) combined.

While BYD is preparing to attempt a run this month, the company shared a video of the Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing in a violent high-speed test.

During the first run, it clocked over 350 km/h (217 mph), no problem. On the second run, it hit over 420 km/h (261 mph).

However, during the third run, BYD was attempting to reach over 450 km/h (280 mph) when the vehicle violently crashed into the guardrail and continued spinning out of control. You can see some of the footage from inside the vehicle.

BYD said that after a comprehensive medical exam, the hospital found the driver in good health with no serious injuries.

When I was still in law enforcement, we did some pursuit driving training and you learn a lot about the dynamics of a vehicle. It's amazing just how quickly and badly something can go wrong at just 100 mph let alone nearly triple that speed. The fact is that the average person can't drive to the max limits of a basic car like a Corolla let alone super cars.

Is it time to reign in the HP and speed wars? Do we need vehicles that can do 0-60 in less than 3 seconds? Unless these companies begin to require 40+ hour specialized training courses in order to buy/operate these high HP vehicles today, then maybe it's time to stop the silly push for more.

And BTW. No matter what the performance levels are of any cars today, I still feel that it would be smart to push legal driving age to at least 17 or 18 instead of 16 and make getting a DL harder to do with way more emphasis on driver's education training.

The vehicle’s high-strength carbon-fiber cabin also held up impressively despite the front and rear damage.

It didn’t take long for BYD to try again, reaching a top speed of 457.89 km/h (284.5 mph) on the next run. Jiang Gong, one of Yangwang’s riders, said he sees some leeway and believes it can break 500 km/h (310 mph).

At the end of the video, BYD said (translated into English), “The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached.”

#4444. Tested: 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma Is a Riot

The Genesis brand’s first performance variant is quick and playful, yet sophisticated.

The Genesis brand’s first performance variant isn’t subtle, particularly when painted in its signature Magma Orange hue. And the ends of its rear wing are turned up, which, to us, gives a devil’s-horns vibe. That’s appropriate, because when driving the Magma, there might as well be a persistent devilish presence on your shoulder whispering, “Push harder.”

The smirks on our faces when driving the Magma are mostly about its immensely swift acceleration, satisfying ride and handling, or the silly-but-impressive 9000-rpm fake engine noises. But the name of this new subbrand also makes us think of “liquid hot magma” (in a Dr. Evil voice, of course).

The GV60 Magma is based on the excellent Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, which introduced the fake shifting and faux engine noises to this electric platform. Peak output is the same 641 horsepower as the Ioniq 5 N, but the Magma gets the full luxury treatment. In fact, the number of Magma-specific touches is staggering for such a low-volume model, including front bucket seats and black suede upholstery with orange stitching—even the key fob dons a Magma Orange shell. Although the front seats are comfortable and supportive, we were surprised to find no lumbar adjustability.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 80219

There are also plenty of Magma-specific displays in the gauge-cluster screen that have a chronograph feel to them. They include information such as the temperatures of the two motors and battery pack, as well as the 9000-rpm tachometer integrated into the speedometer display. Then there are all the configuration settings for the chassis and powertrain modes in the center screen. It’s all thoughtfully and tastefully executed. Plus, there are elements from the regular GV60 that still wow first-timers, such as the circular shifter that flips over and looks like a crystal ball when the car is parked.

While the Ioniq 5 N mimics a 7750-rpm four-cylinder with its engine cosplay, the Magma aims higher, instead playing the tune of a 9000-rpm V-6. Is it gimmicky? Absolutely. But it’s also impressively executed. And loud: With the adjustable noise level turned up all the way, the Magma’s interior volume measures 102 decibels—about the same as a Corvette ZR1X—as it rips its way repeatedly to its pseudo-9000 rpm over and over on the way to a 166-mph top speed.

Despite weighing roughly 90 pounds more, the Magma’s performance is all but identical to the Ioniq 5 N’s, with 60 mph arriving in a scant 3.0 seconds flat and a quarter-mile blitz of 11.1 seconds at 126 mph. The two run neck and neck, at least until the Magma’s longer Boost mode (15 seconds versus 10 in the Ioniq 5 N) causes it to pull ahead above 120 mph. Although there’s a Boost button on the steering wheel, helpfully, the Magma’s extra hit automatically engages when you push the accelerator all the way to the floor.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 80219

Unlike in the Ioniq 5 N, where using the shift mode significantly slows acceleration, Genesis claims no acceleration difference when using the Magma’s fake-shifting mode. With large power cuts between fake shifts, we were highly skeptical. But we measured it both ways, and the Magma does in fact run all but identical times whether faux-shifting or not.

Wearing newer Pirelli P Zero PZ5 Elect summer rubber, versus PZ4 versions on the Ioniq 5 N, the Magma hung on for 0.97 g on the skidpad, slightly exceeding the Ioniq’s 0.96 g. Braking from both 70 mph and 100 mph was pretty much identical.

While you might think that the Magma is an always-on type of car that never settles down—some performance variants can be like that—we were even more impressed at the layers of sophistication on display here. The ride and handling balance in its middle GT mode is terrific even on choppy, undulating roads. Steering is sharp and satisfying. Driven back to back to back against its most obvious competitors—a Cadillac Optiq-V and a Tesla Model Y Performance—the Magma was hands down our favorite. The only part of its dynamic behavior that we didn’t love is a brake pedal that feels slightly squishy as it blends between regen and the brake pads and rotors.

There were some other negatives too. For one, the GV60 Magma entry point is more than 10 grand dearer than the Ioniq 5 N’s, although the Magma’s $72,145 base price is still a relative bargain compared to plenty of other luxury-brand EVs. At highway speeds, the Magma isn’t luxury-car hushed, though, with obvious wind noise, and it measured no quieter (70 decibels and 25 sones) than the Ioniq 5 N when cruising at 70 mph.

Also, the GV60 has a slightly shorter wheelbase than the Ioniq 5, and rear-seat space suffers slightly accordingly. There’s not a lot of foot room under the front seat, and the rear seating height is rather low as well, pushing occupants’ knees upward. Then there’s range. Compared with the least efficient variant of the GV60 line, the Magma is down a significant 45 miles of EPA range, landing at a 222-mile estimate. But that’s a mixed-driving figure, and in our 75-mph highway-range test, the Magma made it only 200 miles.

Is the Magma answering a question many buyers are asking? Clearly not, as Genesis is selling it only at a limited number of dealers in just three states: New York, New Jersey, and California.

But for those who find their way to a Magma, fun is in store.

#4442. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

#4440. Research reveals accelerating sea-level rise around Ireland

A new study led by the ICARUS Climate Research Center at Maynooth University in Ireland has reconstructed a century of Irish sea-level change, revealing a stark acceleration in sea-level rise. The research, titled "A Century of Sea-Level Change in Ireland (1925–2024)" and published in Ocean Science, combines tide-gauge records from six locations, including newly digitized historical records from Cork, Tarbert and Galway.
